lead: Replace the feedback resistor of an inverting amplifier with a capacitor. The virtual ground holds the input end of the capacitor at 0 V, so the current set by the input resistor charges the capacitor. The output becomes proportional to the integral of the input. Swap the resistor and capacitor and the output becomes proportional to the derivative. These two circuits are analog building blocks for proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controllers, analog computers, waveform shaping, edge detection and charge amplifiers. This chapter gives the ideal formulas, the practical fixes for drift and noise, and the frequency response.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for the inverting configuration and virtual ground, and the capacitor relation i = C dv/dt from basic circuit theory.

sections.h3: Ideal integrator: capacitor in the feedback path

blocks.text: Start from the inverting amplifier in Chapter 6.2. The input resistor R₁ carries i = vin/R₁ into the virtual ground. If the feedback element is a capacitor C, that same current must flow into C. The capacitor relation is i = C d(vC)/dt, and vC = 0 − vout = −vout because the left plate is at virtual ground. Therefore vout = −(1/(R₁C))∫vin dt.

blocks.where: v<sub>out</sub> is the output voltage in volts; v<sub>in</sub> is the input voltage in volts; R₁ is the input resistor in ohms; C is the feedback capacitor in farads; R₁C is the time constant in seconds; τ is the dummy time variable in seconds.

blocks.text: The product R₁C is the integrator time constant. A positive step of height V gives a negative ramp: v<sub>out</sub> = −(V/(R₁C))t. A square wave gives a triangle wave. The circuit is called an integrator because the output at time t is the area under the input up to t, scaled by −1/(R₁C).

In the frequency domain the gain magnitude is 1/(ωR₁C), where ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s. Above the corner f = 1/(2πR₁C) the gain falls at 20 dB per decade. A differentiator has the opposite slope: its gain rises at 20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB at the same frequency. The figure uses R₁C = 100 µs, so the crossing is about 1.6 kHz.

An ideal integrator has infinite DC gain. Any op-amp offset voltage or input bias current then charges C without limit, and the output walks to a supply rail. Add a resistor R<sub>f</sub> in parallel with C. At DC the capacitor is open, so the gain is only −R<sub>f</sub>/R₁. The circuit now integrates only above f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C); below f<sub>c</sub> it behaves as an inverting amplifier.

blocks.where: A<sub>DC</sub> is the closed-loop gain at zero frequency in V/V; R<sub>f</sub> is the feedback resistor in ohms; R₁ is the input resistor in ohms.

blocks.text: Choose R<sub>f</sub> large enough not to spoil the integration band but small enough to hold the offset. Add a bias-current compensation resistor from the non-inverting input to ground. Its value is R<sub>comp</sub> = R₁ || R<sub>f</sub>, where || means the parallel combination. At DC this equalises the resistance seen by both inputs, so the bias currents produce nearly the same voltage drop.

Some syllabi call a non-inverting high-input-resistance version a Deboo integrator; it uses a resistor bridge and a capacitor, so the source does not drive R₁ to ground. A charge amplifier is the same idea: a current input flows into C and the output is −q/C, where q is the charge in coulombs; it measures charge from a piezoelectric sensor.

Swap R and C. The input capacitor C feeds the virtual ground, and the feedback resistor R converts the current into voltage. The capacitor current is i = C dv<sub>in</sub>/dt, so v<sub>out</sub> = −R C dv<sub>in</sub>/dt. A triangle input gives a square output because the slope is constant and changes sign at each peak. A sine input gives a cosine output, shifted by 90°.

blocks.where: v<sub>out</sub> is the output voltage in volts; R is the feedback resistor in ohms; C is the input capacitor in farads; dv<sub>in</sub>/dt is the input slope in volts per second.

blocks.text: The ideal differentiator gain rises with frequency without limit. High-frequency noise, stray capacitance and the op-amp's finite gain-bandwidth product (GBP) then dominate; the output can look like noise or oscillate. Add a series resistor R₁ with C. The high-frequency gain is capped at −R/R₁, and the differentiator works below f = 1/(2πR₁C). Add a small capacitor C<sub>f</sub> across R to roll off the gain further.

Use these circuits in PID controllers, analog computers, waveform shaping, edge detection and charge amplifiers. In a PID loop the integrator removes steady error and the differentiator reacts to fast changes. In edge detection a differentiator turns a slow logic transition into a short pulse.

figure.caption: Gain against frequency for an ideal integrator and differentiator with R₁C = 100 µs. The two lines cross 0 dB at about 1.6 kHz; the integrator falls and the differentiator rises at 20 dB per decade.

spec.aria: Gain against frequency for a 100 µs integrator falling at 20 dB per decade and a differentiator rising at 20 dB per decade, both crossing 0 dB at 1.6 kHz.

examples.question: An inverting integrator has R₁ = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 µF. A 1 V step is applied at t = 0. (a) Find R₁C and the ramp slope. (b) Find v_out at t = 1 ms with an ideal op-amp. (c) A differentiator uses the same R and C. Its input is a triangle with slope 1000 V/s. Find its output.
steps: The step height is V = 1 V. The slope is −V/(R₁C) = −1/10⁻⁴ = −10 000 V/s.
At t = 1 ms = 10⁻³ s, v_out = slope × t = −10 000 × 10⁻³ = −10 V.
On ±12 V supplies this ideal value is near the negative rail, so the real output saturates close to 1 ms.
For the differentiator, R C = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁸ = 10⁻⁴ s.
examples.answer: The ideal integrator output at 1 ms is −10 V, and the differentiator output is −0.1 V.
examples.check:
R1 = 10e3
C = 0.01e-6
vin = 1.0
t = 1e-3
tau = R1 * C
slope = -vin / tau
v_out = slope * t
slope_in = 1000.0
v_out_diff = -R1 * C * slope_in
print(v_out)
print(v_out_diff)

traps: Omitting R_f in a practical integrator. Offset voltage and bias current then charge C until the output saturates at a rail.
Saying the integrator output is +(1/(R₁C))∫v_in dt. The inverting input gives a minus sign for a positive step.
Using R₁C in microseconds as if it were seconds. Convert 10 kΩ × 0.01 µF to 100 µs = 10⁻⁴ s first.
Using the ideal differentiator at high frequency. Its gain rises without limit, so noise and stray capacitance dominate; add R₁ in series with C and C_f across R.
Confusing the time constant R₁C with the corner frequency 1/(2πR₁C). The time constant is in seconds; the corner is in hertz.

quiz.q: Write the ideal inverting integrator output formula and define R₁C.
quiz.a: v_out = −(1/(R₁C))∫v_in dt + v_out(0); R₁ is the input resistor in ohms, C is the feedback capacitor in farads, so R₁C is the time constant in seconds.

quiz.q: Why does a practical integrator add R_f across C?
quiz.a: At DC the capacitor C is open. Without R_f the DC gain is infinite, so offset voltage and bias current drive the output to a rail. R_f sets the DC gain to −R_f/R₁ and holds the output.

quiz.q: An integrator has R₁ = 20 kΩ, C = 0.05 µF, and a 2 V step input. Find the ramp slope and v_out at 0.5 ms.
A differentiator has R = 100 kΩ and C = 0.001 µF. Its input is a triangle with slope 500 V/s. Find v_out.
A 10 kHz, 10 mV sine noise reaches the differentiator in the previous question. Find the noise output amplitude and compare it with the 500 V/s triangle result.
quiz.a: dv/dt amplitude = 10 mV × 2π × 10 kHz = 10 × 10⁻³ × 6.283 × 10⁴ = 628.3 V/s. Output amplitude = 10⁻⁴ × 628.3 = 0.0628 V = 62.8 mV. Noise is larger than the 50 mV signal; this is why practical differentiators need R₁ and C_f.

quiz.q: Explain how finite GBP and stray capacitance affect an ideal differentiator, and how R₁ and C_f help.
quiz.a: Ideal gain rises with frequency. Finite GBP makes the op-amp run out of loop gain, adding phase shift and flattening or peaking the response; stray capacitance at the input and feedback path increases high-frequency gain. Series R₁ caps gain at −R/R₁ and sets a corner 1/(2πR₁C); C_f across R rolls off the highest frequencies.

quiz.q: Sketch the gain against frequency of an ideal integrator and differentiator. Mark the 0 dB crossing.
quiz.a: The integrator line falls at 20 dB/decade; the differentiator line rises at 20 dB/decade. Both cross 0 dB at f = 1/(2πRC). For RC = 100 µs, f ≈ 1.6 kHz.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, integrators appear in PID loop filters, charge amplifiers for piezoelectric sensors, and active-filter building blocks. Differentiators appear in edge detectors, FM demodulators and rate-of-change alarms. Modern design adds finite-GBP compensation and input bias-current selection. Search for 'practical op-amp integrator offset', 'differentiator noise gain' and 'charge amplifier reset switch'.
